beats.headline: The Ping carried people and goods through the valley
beats.body: One documented journey from Bangkok to Chiang Mai took about three months upstream, including a month working through thirty-two rapids. The river was vital, seasonal and difficult.

beats.headline: Caravans crossed the mountains by many routes
beats.body: Mule caravans linked Chiang Mai with the trading worlds of southwest China. Their paths shifted with season, water, security and politics, so the map shows a corridor rather than a single road.

beats.headline: The highway arrived on a new alignment
beats.body: Highway 11 entered Chiang Mai from the south-east as the last section of the Superhighway. It was not a caravan trail paved over, but a new layer of connection across the valley.

beats.headline: The railway turned a journey into a timetable
beats.body: The Northern Line reached Chiang Mai through the 1,352-metre Khun Tan tunnel. A journey once governed by rapids, water levels and season could now run on fixed tracks and a timetable.

beats.headline: Remote work brought a connection with no route
beats.body: By the mid-2010s, people could live in Chiang Mai while working for somewhere else. Unlike river, road or rail, that connection had no surveyable line — the seam where the mapped past runs out.

hotspots.label: Chiang Mai railway station
hotspots.blurb: The national terminus landed 1.57 km from Wat Ket.
hotspots.body: Rail arrived almost on top of the older river-commercial landscape. A new long-distance network connected to the old one here.

hotspots.label: Khun Tan tunnel
hotspots.blurb: A tunnel through 1,352 metres of mountain.
hotspots.body: Building it was dangerous and disease-prone. The often-repeated claim that more than a thousand people died there has never been firmly verified.

hotspots.label: Chiang Mai airport
hotspots.blurb: Air travel added another route into the valley.
hotspots.body: Air travel added another way into the valley. Decades later, it became one of the conditions that allowed people to stay in Chiang Mai while their work remained somewhere else.

beats.headline: The circle starts here
beats.body: The raised cells show where people live. Wat Ket is the point from which this chapter measures distance.

beats.headline: Half of humanity lives within this distance of Wat Ket
beats.body: At 1,000 km the circle holds 3.6% of the world's population. At 2,000 km it holds 20.1%. By about 3,400 km from Wat Ket, it reaches half.
beats.footnote: With a world total of 8.0 billion, the half-population radius is 3,416 km. It is 3,303 km at 7.8 billion and 3,524 km at 8.2 billion; the headline rounds to about 3,400 km.

beats.headline: After halfway, the curve flattens
beats.body: At 6,000 km the circle holds 59.5% of the world's population. Beyond halfway, each extra kilometre brings relatively few more people inside.

hotspots.label: Wat Ket
hotspots.blurb: Move the centre here and the answer barely changes.
hotspots.body: The older Valeriepieris circle has a radius of 3,437 km and is centred about 280 km away. Re-centering the calculation on Wat Ket changes the distance very little: the story here is how far the circle travels, not a claim that Wat Ket is a special mathematical centre.

beats.headline: This is one possible Chiang Mai in 2045
beats.body: The newspaper and the places pinned here belong to one possible Chiang Mai in 2045. Follow the pins to see how its residents learn, farm, travel and work.

beats.headline: A weir shares the flow without stopping the river
beats.body: A fai slows water and sends some of it through smaller channels while the river continues downstream. Across this Chiang Mai, communities connect with the world while keeping control of their land, skills and institutions.

beats.headline: Craft training pays the teacher, not the institution
beats.body: Apprentices enter through a named Master and a community trust. Every funded foreign place supports a Thai place too, while the people who hold the craft keep the final say.

beats.headline: Local and international children share one school system
beats.body: Lanna World School is a joint demonstration school of all eight Chiang Mai universities. Thai sits at the core of the curriculum, with English, Mandarin and an IB year opening outward from it.

beats.headline: The valley connects these places
beats.body: Schools and workshops in the city sit among farms, forests and neighbouring towns. Pull back to see how food, skills and care move through the wider valley.

beats.headline: A festival asks its crowd to be still
beats.body: L-Pop leaves long stretches of silence around a low resonance measured along the ridge. Its clinicians offer a pause for the nervous system, then point people towards the slower work of healing elsewhere.

beats.headline: Highland tea reaches buyers in three languages
beats.body: At one tea business, Thai connects the growers, Mandarin reaches Kunming and English reaches other buyers. The crop travels through distant markets while cultivation stays in the mountains.

beats.headline: The farm's best idea outlives the farm
beats.body: The uncareering farm is closing, and its tool libraries, kitchens and mutual credit already operate elsewhere. The land returns to agriculture, while buildings remain in use by farmers and apprentices.

beats.headline: Farmers share the machines that carry their harvest
beats.body: Villages elect dispatchers and earn flight time by maintaining drones and solar stations. The machines carry shade-grown crops down steep slopes, making forest farming practical without clearing the hills.

beats.headline: Disaster response brings skills back to the valley
beats.body: KAE's multilingual crews travel to floods, fires and difficult terrain across borders. The organisation trains specialists and publishes open methods, so relief work also builds capacity in northern Thailand.

hotspots.label: Ban Tawan
hotspots.blurb: The trust that learned not to scale.
hotspots.body: Journeyfolk limits each Master to three apprentices because the scarce resource is attention. Outside money pays people to teach, but the trust keeps control over who enters and how the system grows.

hotspots.label: Wua Lai
hotspots.blurb: The 5,000th Journeyfolk Mark leaves the silver quarter.
hotspots.body: A lineage mark follows every registered piece: Master, apprentice and village. The system exports people and relationships more readily than it exports ownership of the craft itself.

hotspots.label: Lanna World School
hotspots.blurb: One school for the city's children and the world's.
hotspots.body: Thai national education, three languages and an international diploma sit inside the same institution. Its graduates do not have to choose between being rooted here and working across borders.

hotspots.label: Anusarn
hotspots.blurb: The school spreads through the city instead of retreating behind a gate.
hotspots.body: Lanna World School uses more than one site rather than separating itself into an enclosed international campus. The neighbourhood remains part of the education.

hotspots.label: KAE, Wiang Kum Kam
hotspots.blurb: Climate response became an industry of its own.
hotspots.body: KAE sends multilingual field teams wherever floods, fires and other climate emergencies overwhelm local capacity. Its open methods and training networks bring relief money and specialist skills back through northern Thailand.

hotspots.label: Wat Umong
hotspots.blurb: Waste for Merit turns rubbish back into neighbourhood resources.
hotspots.body: Food scraps become compost for the temple food forest. Recyclables feed a small fabrication lab, while service and teaching can be exchanged for food without every transaction passing through money.

hotspots.label: Doi Suthep
hotspots.blurb: At L-Pop, the mountain is the headliner.
hotspots.body: The festival is built around long silences and a low-frequency resonance measured along the ridge. Its clinicians call it regulation rather than cure: a place to quiet the nervous system before slower work continues elsewhere.

hotspots.label: Doi Saket
hotspots.blurb: The farm that invented uncareering is closing.
hotspots.body: Its tool libraries, kitchens and mutual-credit practices have spread far beyond the place that began them. The land returns to agriculture because the institution has become less necessary than the habits it helped create.

hotspots.label: Lamphun hills
hotspots.blurb: The drones work because the village owns the system.
hotspots.body: Farmers pool repairs, maintain shared solar stations and earn flight time by working on the network. The drones carry shade-grown crops down steep slopes, making forest farming practical without clearing the mountain.

hotspots.label: Lamphun
hotspots.body: Lamphun is an early member of the Ping Plexus, now a network of 67 districts. Its basic rule is that hospitality should run both ways: communities that receive mobile people should gain routes outward too.

hotspots.label: Mae Taeng
hotspots.blurb: Highland tea travels farther than the people growing it.
hotspots.body: Growers work across local farms and distant markets without moving production out of the mountains. Thai, Mandarin and English carry the crop through different parts of the same trading network.

hotspots.label: Chiang Dao
hotspots.blurb: 64 km north, beyond the edge of this map.
hotspots.body: Shared drones work as flying pack mules for forest-grown crops in the highlands. The Ping Pass carries a different kind of route outward: slow, reciprocal travel through the wider Plexus.
